Lucius Verus. A Roman emperor and co-ruler with Marcus Aurelius during the early Antonine period, from one hundred thirty to one hundred sixty-nine CE. Adopted by Emperor Antoninus Pius as a potential heir, he shared imperial power with his brother Marcus Aurelius from one hundred sixty-one to one hundred sixty-nine CE in a unique experiment in dual rulership that generally functioned well despite their strikingly different personalities.

He was adopted by Emperor Antoninus Pius along with the young Marcus Aurelius, both groomed as potential heirs to stabilize the succession. Upon Antoninus Pius's death in one hundred sixty-one CE, both adopted sons became emperors, creating a rare dual-reign arrangement that the Senate accepted without significant controversy.

Lucius Verus personally commanded Roman forces during the Parthian War from one hundred sixty-two to one hundred sixty-six CE, achieving military victories but also exposing the empire to plague and disease from the East. He contrasted sharply with his co-emperor Marcus Aurelius. While Marcus Aurelius devoted himself to Stoic philosophy and righteous governance, Lucius Verus pursued pleasure, entertainment, and martial glory.

Despite their contrasting temperaments, the two worked effectively together, dividing responsibilities so that each handled matters suited to his talents and inclinations. He died in one hundred sixty-nine CE, possibly from plague or overexertion, leaving Marcus Aurelius as sole emperor and setting up the succession of the troubled Commodus.

Lucius Verus shares a co-rulership with Marcus Aurelius his adopted brother, whose philosophical temperament balanced his martial and hedonistic inclinations, and connects to the Roman Empire the institution he briefly helped govern during the prosperous Antonine period.
